title: How teeth and jaws work together
intro: Teeth and jaws form a precise system for biting, chewing, speaking and smiling. The upper and lower teeth meet in a pattern called the bite, and the jaw joints and chewing muscles move the lower jaw. When the parts fit together well, chewing is efficient and forces are shared evenly.

sections.heading: The parts of a tooth
paragraphs: A tooth has a hard white outer layer called enamel, which is the hardest substance in the body, and a softer layer underneath called dentine. Inside is the pulp, containing nerves and blood vessels. The root anchors the tooth in the jawbone through fibres that act as a flexible cushion.

sections.heading: Different teeth, different jobs
paragraphs: Adults normally have 32 teeth, including wisdom teeth. Incisors at the front cut food, canines tear, and premolars and molars crush and grind. Children first have 20 baby teeth, which begin to be replaced by permanent teeth at about six years of age and hold space for the permanent ones.

sections.heading: The jaw joints and muscles
paragraphs: The lower jaw connects to the skull at two temporomandibular joints, just in front of the ears. Strong chewing muscles open, close and move the jaw sideways. The joints can both hinge and glide, which lets you grind food.
Clenching or grinding the teeth, an injury or arthritis may cause jaw pain, clicking or limited opening. Many such problems improve with self-care, physiotherapy or a bite splint.

sections.heading: What a good bite looks like
paragraphs: In a well-aligned bite, the upper teeth slightly overlap the lower ones, and the molars interlock. Crowded, gapped or misaligned teeth can make cleaning harder and sometimes affect chewing and speech, but not every deviation needs treatment.
Missing teeth can allow neighbouring teeth to drift, which changes the bite over time. Replacements such as bridges, dentures or implants help to maintain function.

sections.heading: Looking after teeth and jaws
paragraphs: Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, clean between the teeth daily, limit sugary snacks and drinks, and see a dentist regularly. Seek advice for persistent jaw pain, difficulty opening your mouth, loose teeth or bleeding gums.

examples.title: Noticing jaw clicking
examples.text: Imagine your jaw clicks when you open wide but does not hurt. You could mention it at your next dental visit, and ask whether any treatment is needed and which habits, like chewing gum for hours, are worth changing.

examples.title: Talking about night grinding
examples.text: Suppose your partner hears you grinding your teeth at night and you wake with sore jaw muscles. You might ask your dentist about a protective splint and ways to manage stress.
